Getting started

Organize your transcripts and credits before building a degree plan

You can start planning before every transcript arrives. Build an honest inventory from what you know, mark missing records, and refine the plan when original records and school evaluations are available.

DegreeSteps editorial team5 min readReviewed 2026-11-01

On this page

  1. Start with a short source checklist
  2. Use one row per original learning record
  3. Keep credit units and statuses clear
  4. Use the CSV template as a structure
  5. Preview before importing or sharing
  6. Refine the provisional plan

Put this into a plan.

Build my degree path

Start with a short source checklist

List every college or university attended, including schools where you did not finish a degree. Add exam providers, alternative-course providers, military education records, and relevant certificates or workplace training. A course that did not help one earlier degree may still be worth evaluating for a new target.

Collect the unofficial copies you can access for planning and identify how to request the official versions the receiving school requires. Keep the original source visible. A previous school’s transfer summary may not provide the course detail or direct documentation that the next school needs.

Use one row per original learning record

For a college course or exam, record the provider, course or exam code, title, credit amount, credit system, status, and completion date when known. Use the names and identifiers on the source record rather than inventing a university equivalent. The degree audit is where proposed receiving placements belong.

For military or certificate learning, preserve the credential identity and version or date information needed for evaluation. Do not turn a broad training description into guessed academic credits. Keep a note that a record needs review when it does not fit a simple course row.

Keep credit units and statuses clear

Semester and quarter credits are different units. Preserve the original unit and let a documented receiving-school conversion govern an award. Avoid changing a number just to make it fit a degree worksheet. Do the same for completed, in-progress, and planned work: they communicate different facts.

An earned source record does not automatically establish a school-confirmed requirement placement. If you have a written evaluation, keep it associated with the particular program and requirement. If you do not, record the course as completed and let the placement remain pending.

Use the CSV template as a structure

DegreeSteps’s CSV import template uses nine columns: provider, code, title, credits, creditSystem, status, grade, score, and completedOn. An Excel template and transcript upload are also available. Both spreadsheet templates are blank; the displayed examples are guides to filling them in. Keep the header names and one record per row. Review the importer’s column instructions for accepted status values and date format.

As an illustrative record, a finished community-college algebra course would use the college as provider, its actual course code and title, the original credit amount and unit, an earned status, and its actual completion date. That record does not claim equivalency to a destination’s algebra requirement. The receiving placement is a separate decision.

Preview before importing or sharing

Check that each column landed in the right place and that the record count matches what you intended. Correct titles or codes from your source records before confirming. An edited file should receive a new preview so you are approving the current data rather than a stale version.

A transcript can contain sensitive personal information that a learning inventory does not need. Do not add student identification numbers, home addresses, birth dates, or private advising messages to a course CSV or public community post. A reusable public plan can describe proposed courses without publishing your original personal records.

Refine the provisional plan

Once the inventory is ready, choose an exact degree or compare suitable targets. The first useful output is a list of potentially applicable learning and the records or answers still needed. A rough estimate such as “about a year of college” can guide a conversation, but it should not be subtracted from degree requirements as confirmed credit.

When official evaluations arrive, update the relevant placements and keep the original learning intact. Add new completions over time rather than rebuilding the whole inventory whenever you compare a school. A small, well-labeled file is enough to begin; accuracy improves through original records and specific school decisions.

Sources & further reading

  • ACE: transcripts and original learning documentation
  • WGU: transcript submission and evaluation guidance
  • Liberty: residential transfer and credit-unit information
  • VA: obtaining military education records
Use this as a starting point.

Policies and individual degree requirements can change. Confirm the exact course, catalog, and placement with the receiving school before paying for new learning.
